content: Atopic eczema (AE) is a chronic, non-infectious inflammatory skin condition characterized by an itchy, red rash. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of dietary exclusions as a treatment for established atopic eczema. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, PsycINFO, AMED, and ISI Web of Science, up to March 2006. Additional searches were performed on clinical trial registries and pharmaceutical companies were contacted for unpublished data. The inclusion criteria required participants to have a physician-confirmed diagnosis of atopic eczema. Two independent reviewers selected studies and assessed their methodological quality. The review identified nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 421 participants. Of these, six studies investigated the exclusion of egg and milk (N=288), one study examined a few foods diet (N=85), and two studies evaluated an elemental diet (N=48). The findings indicated no significant benefit of an eggand milk-free diet in unselected participants with atopic eczema. Similarly, there was no evidence to support the use of an elemental diet or a few foods diet in unselected cases of atopic eczema. However, there may be some benefit to an egg-free diet in infants with suspected egg allergy who have positive specific IgE to eggs. One study reported that 51% of children on an egg-free diet showed significant improvement in the percentage of body surface area affected by eczema compared to those on a normal diet (relative risk [RR] 1.51, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07 to 2.11). Additionally, improvements in surface area and severity scores were observed at the end of six weeks (mean difference [MD] 5.50, 95% CI 0.19 to 10.81) and at the end of treatment (MD 6.10, 95% CI 0.06 to 12.14). The interpretation of these findings is limited by methodological issues, including poor concealment of randomization, lack of blinding, and high dropout rates without intention-to-treat analysis. These limitations necessitate cautious interpretation of the results. In conclusion, while there may be some benefit to an egg-free diet in infants with suspected egg allergy and positive specific IgE to eggs, there is little evidence to support the use of exclusion diets in unselected individuals with atopic eczema. This lack of evidence may be due to the fact that many participants were not allergic to the excluded substances or because the studies were underpowered and poorly reported. Future research should focus on adequately powered studies involving participants with confirmed food allergies. Additionally, it is important to differentiate between young children, whose food allergies may resolve over time, and older children or adults.
